video_title: There's a Mind-Boggling Number of Rich People in America | Odd Lots
gist: Two economists (Owen, Princeton; Eric, Chicago Booth), authors of 'The Everywhere Millionaire', built a first-of-its-kind linked IRS dataset connecting pass-through businesses to their owners and workers, and found that the top of the US income distribution is dominated not by tech billionaires but by millions of mid-market private business owners: auto dealers, beer distributors, dentists, doctors, contractors and regional manufacturers. They argue pass-through business income drives more than half the rise in top-1% income share since the 1980s, that much of it rests on local regulatory rents rather than invention, and that reform is blocked partly because roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through owners.

insights.claim: Pass-through entities (S corps, partnerships) escape the corporate tax entirely, sending profits and losses straight to owners, and after Reagan's 1986 reform made top individual rates lower than corporate rates they became the dominant organizational form, now accounting for the vast majority of US businesses and roughly half of all business profits.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth professor of economics and finance)
insights.so_what: Any analysis of US corporate profitability or effective tax rates built only on C-corp/public-company data is missing about half the business sector, and tax-reform headlines aimed at 'corporations' may leave the larger pool untouched.
insights.quote: after Reagan cut taxes in 1986 for an individual is lower than corporations. That suddenly became the most attractive way to organize yourself.

insights.claim: Pass-through business income is among the most concentrated income in America: about 70 cents of every dollar of it accrues to the top 1% of earners.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Changes to pass-through tax treatment are functionally top-1% tax policy, regardless of the 'small business' framing used to sell them.

insights.claim: More than half the growth in the famous Piketty-Saez top-1% income share from the 1980s through 2021 comes in the form of pass-through business income rather than wages or traditional capital income.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: The single biggest driver of measured US income inequality is a tax-structure phenomenon, which means inequality is more policy-reversible than a pure technology or globalization story implies.

insights.claim: An anesthesiologist running income through an S corp pays materially less tax than an identically-skilled salaried anesthesiologist, avoiding payroll tax and the uncapped ACA Medicare surcharge on everything above a vague 'reasonable compensation' wage floor.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: The tax code pays a large premium for being an owner rather than an employee doing the same work, a wedge that steadily pushes high-earning professionals out of salaried employment and into private practice and PE-backed rollups.

insights.claim: Doctors who bill Medicare heavily often avoid paying Medicare tax on the bulk of what is economically their own labor income by routing it through a pass-through entity.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: A concrete fiscal leak to watch if Medicare financing reform returns to the agenda: the provider class funding the program least is also billing it most.
insights.quote: Which is maybe particularly galling because they're billing Medicare for so much services. And they themselves on their mostly labor income aren't paying the Medicare tax on it.

insights.claim: The 2017 tax reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30% and added guardrails excluding doctors and skilled service professions, but practitioners work around them by shifting income into ancillary services, surgical entities, or real estate rented back to the practice.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Occupation-based guardrails on tax benefits are porous; income-based caps are the only structurally robust limit, which matters for handicapping the design of any future reform.

insights.claim: States have let pass-through owners take state and local tax deductions at the entity level, escaping the SALT cap that still binds salaried workers on identical income.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: The SALT cap is far less binding than headline analysis assumes for business owners, weakening the revenue estimates and the distributional case around it.
insights.quote: But if you run all your income through the business, then the states have allowed them to basically take the deductions through the business instead and get that uncapped.

insights.claim: The pass-through loophole structure is best understood as depreciation on the tax code: an asset that decays as the economy evolves and tax-optimization strategies advance, and which requires deliberate periodic repair rather than only being cut further.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: A reusable model for forecasting tax policy: absent active maintenance, effective rates on structurable income ratchet down over time regardless of statutory rates.
insights.quote: I like to think of the tax code like a house that sort of depreciates over time.

insights.claim: Salaried W-2 workers are the only significant class of earners with no obvious mechanism to minimize their tax bill.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Frames why any broad-based revenue increase keeps landing on wages, and why the wage-vs-owner tax wedge keeps widening.
insights.quote: the only sort of class of people that really does not have some, like, very obvious way to minimize taxes is basically just workers

themes.theme: Who is actually rich in America

insights.claim: For every large public-company CEO in America there are roughly a thousand private business owners holding $25 million or more, a layer of wealth almost entirely absent from public discussion of inequality.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Wealth-management, private banking, luxury goods and private-market fundraising TAMs are anchored in regional private owners, not in the Forbes 400 or C-suite comp.
insights.quote: there's a thousand private business owners that have $25 million for every large public company CEO. Like, we've missed all of these people.

insights.claim: The top of the US income distribution is dominated by mid-market regional operating businesses numbering in the millions, not by monopolistic big-business rentiers passively collecting capital income.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Reframes the inequality debate from financial-capital accumulation toward active business ownership, which changes which policy levers (tax structure, licensing, franchise law) actually bite.

insights.claim: Unlike Piketty's picture of a faceless top 1% earning passive returns on accumulated financial capital, the real US rich hold concentrated, undiversified portfolios in which the operating business is the main asset and human capital — networks, experience, contracts, market position — is a critical input.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Implies top-end wealth is far less liquid and far more idiosyncratic than market-based wealth estimates suggest, with direct consequences for wealth-tax feasibility and for succession-driven deal flow.
insights.quote: our book is kind of like picketing with people

insights.claim: Because IRS tax data cannot identify individuals by name, the researchers located specific wealthy pass-through owners by cross-referencing yacht and private jet registration records against the industry signatures their tax analysis had flagged.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: A replicable research method for mapping private wealth where no public disclosure exists, useful for anyone sourcing LPs, sellers or private-market counterparties.

insights.claim: You can become a billionaire in a brutally competitive industry with no market power at all, as demonstrated by a Chicago hot dog operator who started washing dishes by hand without running water and built the business over decades while owning all the real estate, taking no debt and reinvesting every dollar.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Cuts against the reflex that extreme wealth requires monopoly rents; the operating model — own the real estate, avoid leverage, reinvest — is itself the compounding mechanism.

insights.claim: Getting rich in these businesses is a decades-long grind rather than a fast scaling exercise, the opposite of the Silicon Valley model.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Explains why this wealth cohort is old, concentrated in illiquid assets and now hitting succession age — the setup for the entire lower-middle-market M&A opportunity.
insights.quote: in contrast to the Silicon Valley, move fast and break things. It's off and move slow and make things. It takes decades, often.

insights.claim: First-generation private business founders in this cohort characteristically have no hobbies and cannot sit still, exemplified by an entrepreneur who tried retiring to golf in Florida, got bored, and started a $5 electric toothbrush company during the dot-com era that made him hundreds of millions.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton professor of economics)
insights.so_what: A behavioral screen for acquirers and investors backing operators: relentlessness rather than idea quality is the recurring trait in this wealth cohort.

insights.claim: Auto dealers are the single largest industry bucket generating pass-through business income within the top 0.1% of earners, ahead of tech and finance.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Dealership groups deserve attention as a wealth and political-influence pool wildly disproportionate to their share of public-market capitalization.
insights.quote: the auto dealers were the number one bucket, which we were like, okay, this is not the Piketty story of like billionaire tech or finance.

insights.claim: A third-generation Florida Mercedes dealer family sold their dealership for several hundred million dollars to a consortium co-owned by Nick Saban and then spent roughly $60 million on their daughter's wedding, flying guests to Paris and renting Versailles — and they are not close to the top of the list of the country's most prodigious car dealers.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Concrete calibration for dealership exit multiples and the scale of liquidity events happening well below public-market visibility.

insights.claim: State franchise laws originally written to protect small dealers from manufacturers now create local monopolies: manufacturers cannot open a competing Toyota store within a geographic boundary of an existing dealership and have very limited power to introduce competition.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: Dealership cash flows are legally protected rents, which supports high acquisition multiples but also makes the sector a standing target if regional antitrust or direct-to-consumer auto sales gain traction.

insights.claim: By 2008 Chrysler had roughly three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, because franchise protections required paying dealers off — including years of rent — to close them.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: A hard historical measure of how much deadweight franchise protection creates, and of the cost any future OEM restructuring must absorb.

insights.claim: Dealer profitability comes less from the vehicle sale than from ancillary services — financing, warranties and repair — where markups are far higher and the dealer enjoys a first-mover advantage because the customer is already on the lot.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Any disruption that unbundles auto financing or warranties from the point of sale attacks the actual profit pool, not the visible one.

insights.claim: Competition and antitrust problems in the US are heavily regionalized rather than national, concentrated in locally protected franchises and distributorships instead of big national-scale companies.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Antitrust enforcement aimed at national platforms may be pointed at the wrong layer of the economy; the durable rents sit in state-law-protected local chokepoints.

insights.claim: Beer distributors — not brewers — own the branded delivery trucks, and post-Prohibition three-tier state laws force product through protected middle-tier contracts, making distributors incredibly wealthy as beer demand grows.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: A textbook toll-booth business model protected by state statute: high, stable, legally-moated cash flows that rarely appear in public-market screens.
insights.quote: these are incredibly wealthy businesses that sit between manufacturers and end users, like bars, restaurants, groceries, and so on

insights.claim: A rule designed to stop big brewers from dominating distribution instead transferred durable pricing power to the distributors, who over time became big guys themselves — visible in private-jet data, with a San Antonio mayor remarking he had never seen so many jets at the airport as when the beer wholesalers held their conference.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Illustrates the general failure mode of protective regulation: the protected intermediary becomes the rent extractor, which is where the wealth and lobbying power accumulate.

insights.claim: Doctors' offices rank as the number one four-digit industry code by profits within the top 1% of earners, out of roughly 300 four-digit service industries.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Physician practice ownership is the largest single top-end income engine in the US, which is why PE rollups keep targeting it and why physician-fee policy is politically untouchable.

insights.claim: Dentists rank around number 21 on the list of top pass-through four-digit industries by profit, and total US dentist revenue exceeds the combined revenue of the NFL, NBA and MLB.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: A vivid scale check: unglamorous fragmented healthcare services dwarf the industries that dominate media coverage, making them the natural consolidation target.
insights.quote: if you add up all the revenue of dentists in America, it exceeds the revenue generated by the NFL, the NBA, MLB

insights.claim: Dentists exist in every congressional district and lobby against measures like adding dental services to Medicare specifically to avoid government price pressure.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Geographic dispersion, not size, is the source of lobbying power here — a signal for handicapping the odds of dental or healthcare benefit expansion.
insights.quote: they lobby against that to be like, well we don't want price pressure from the government

insights.claim: The US has roughly 30% fewer doctors than the OECD average because the American Medical Association helps restrict physician supply, letting practice owners raise prices as demand grows while nurses and assistants capture little of the surplus.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Supply restriction is a direct mechanical driver of both healthcare cost inflation and top-1% income growth — worth watching as a policy variable for both.

insights.claim: Dentists are classic soft targets for film financiers and other promoters because they sit on large pools of cash with few ideas of what to do with it.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Identifies where unsophisticated retail-scale risk capital actually comes from, relevant to anyone mapping the buyer base for alternative and private offerings.
insights.quote: They are, I think, sitting on pools of cash. Uh, and maybe they don't have so many ideas of what to do with it. And so they make for maybe easy targets.

insights.claim: More than half the typical deals in a private equity pipeline are founder-owned firms with no natural successor, meaning PE's real business is buying unglamorous regional operators — cabinet manufacturers, plumbing companies, shade stores — rather than glamorous transactions.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: PE deal flow is fundamentally a demographic succession trade, so the supply of deals tracks boomer retirement rather than credit cycles or public-market valuations.
insights.quote: I'm going to work for a prestigious private equity firm in San Francisco so I can run their plumbing company in Mississippi

insights.claim: Tens of trillions of dollars sit in the silent and baby boomer generations' wealth and more than half of it is business wealth, much of it in firms too small to attract private equity interest and with no family successor.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the runway for search funds and independent sponsors: the sub-PE segment of the succession wave is still largely unserved.

insights.claim: The median search fund return is negative because most searches simply fail to find a business, while the average return is in the low 20s — an option-like payoff distribution for the investors who fund the search and then fund the acquisition in a second step.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Search funds only work as a diversified portfolio bet; a single-deal allocation is a coin flip, and the reported average return hides a mostly-losing median.
insights.quote: even the median return in search funds is negative. Most of them lose a little bit of money because the search doesn't work, but the average return is like, um, low 20s

insights.claim: Search fund acquisitions are financed mostly with bank debt at roughly 40-50% leverage rather than the 80% typical of larger LBOs, leaving materially more equity cushion.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Lower-middle-market buyouts should be far less rate-sensitive and less default-prone than sponsor-backed large caps, a useful distinction when assessing private credit risk.

insights.claim: The most successful search-fund cases cited include pest control rollups and a California drug treatment facility that returned roughly 100x, where the edge came from operational complexity — billing and regulatory management — rather than from the product.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Regulatory and billing complexity is the moat in these rollups, so screening should favor operationally messy sectors rather than clean ones.

insights.claim: About 60% of US business sector growth over the last 25 years has come in pass-through form, so the pie genuinely grew — but the owners' share of it rose from roughly a third or 40% to about 50%.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Rising inequality here is roughly half real value creation and half redistribution toward owners, which cuts against both the pure-rent and pure-productivity narratives.

insights.claim: Value added per worker in these businesses rose from about $34,000 in 2001 to about $52,000 in 2021, and owners captured roughly $15,000 of that $18,000 increase.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: The single hardest number in the episode: workers received roughly one-sixth of two decades of productivity gains in the pass-through sector, which is the mechanical source of the wealth layer being described.
insights.quote: there's 18 K per worker of growth owners got 15 of that and workers got the rest

insights.claim: Profit sharing is simply not the default mindset of first-generation founders, who pay workers for defined tasks and reinvest or keep the residual, so productivity gains from offshoring or process improvement flow to the owner rather than to labor.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Ownership structure, not just technology, determines who captures productivity gains — relevant to forecasting labor share as private ownership expands.

insights.claim: Part of the owner share gain is genuine scarce expertise rather than rents, illustrated by a star economics consultant whose work raising the probability of a $1 billion merger by a few percent is worth enormous sums as the economy and merger values grow.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: Scale effects mean the same expert skill is worth far more as transaction sizes grow, an underappreciated mechanism behind top-end professional incomes.

insights.claim: Roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners, which is the core reason these loopholes persist through successive reform attempts.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: A structural, quantified reason to discount any forecast that pass-through tax preferences will be curtailed, regardless of which party holds power.
insights.quote: it turns out that like a quarter of federal elected officials are also past their business owners

insights.claim: Only about 20% of total pass-through income actually comes from small business according to an old Treasury study; the vast majority comes from large businesses that simply happen to be privately held.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: The 'small business' defense of pass-through tax breaks is empirically false for 80% of the dollars at stake — the single most useful fact for anyone modeling future tax reform.
insights.quote: if you take all passthrough income, only 20% of it is actually small business

insights.claim: The most realistic reform path is not eliminating pass-through loopholes but capping them by income level — for instance denying the deduction above $1 million of business income — since anyone above that threshold cannot plausibly be called small.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: If a revenue-raising package ever materializes, an income-threshold cap on the pass-through deduction is the most likely structural form to prepare for.

insights.claim: Even Democratic congressional staffers show reticence about touching the trillion-dollar pass-through tax cut in the 'one big beautiful bill' because of the small-business framing, making the largest available revenue source politically inert.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Fiscal forecasts assuming a future bipartisan revenue grab from the wealthy should discount this pool heavily; it is off the table for both parties.

insights.claim: A bipartisan Social Security shoring-up proposal from Senators Bernie Moreno and Elizabeth Warren would fund the program off salaried workers' payroll while making no mention of very wealthy pass-through business owners — and Moreno himself was an auto dealer.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: A live, current example that entitlement financing proposals continue to target wages and exempt business income — the burden falls on W-2 earners even in bipartisan packages.

insights.claim: Car dealers' outsized political influence within congressional districts is reasonably well understood, but the same structure replicated across dozens of other protected industries — beverage distribution, dentistry, contracting — represents an unappreciated bloc of political power over the tax code.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: The lobbying resistance to tax and competition reform is far broader and more geographically distributed than the visible auto-dealer lobby suggests.

insights.claim: A newly built dataset linking every US business to its owners and workers allows tracking every new firm in America since 2000, producing the best entrepreneurship data that has ever existed.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: Signals a coming wave of empirical work on private business formation and returns that will likely overturn current consensus estimates of US wealth composition.

insights.claim: A poor child raised in Salt Lake City is roughly three times more likely to start a top-decile business by revenue or employment than an equivalent child raised in Mississippi, with the possible mechanism being Mormon missionary work building door-knocking resilience.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: Entrepreneurship rates are shaped by local culture and exposure rather than capital access alone, which matters for where regional business formation and future deal supply concentrates.

insights.claim: Children of business owners are far more likely to start businesses themselves even after removing all family firms from the data, so the transmission is exposure and know-how rather than inheritance.
insights.speaker: Owen (co-author, Princeton)
insights.so_what: Business-ownership advantage compounds across generations through non-financial channels, meaning wealth taxes or estate taxes alone would not disrupt the mechanism.

insights.claim: The original Treasury-commissioned project stalled because IRS business forms and investor forms use identifiers that were never designed to be linked, and no documentation existed — the researchers ultimately solved it over lunch with the individual who designed the XML filing system.
insights.speaker: Eric (co-author, Chicago Booth)
insights.so_what: Treasury lacked the basic capacity to measure how much tax pass-throughs pay, which means official distributional scoring of past tax bills rested on far weaker data than assumed.
insights.quote: There's no documentation. There's just like this knowledge in people's brains that you have to find to try and do this link.
